summaries.example: Imagine you say, “I feel nervous about the test.” You might know this from noticing your feeling, thinking about the test, or seeing how you act. But you might also misunderstand yourself. For example, you may think you dislike a class when you are really worried about one difficult assignment. Philosophers ask which way of finding out is most trustworthy.
summaries.summary: Self-knowledge means knowing what is happening in your own mind. This includes knowing your feelings, thoughts, beliefs, wants, and plans. Philosophers disagree about what makes this kind of knowledge special. Maybe it is more certain than knowledge of the outside world. Maybe only you can use the special method needed to find it. Maybe your ability to make choices gives you a special connection to your beliefs and intentions. Another idea is that people are treated as authorities about their own minds because of ordinary ways of speaking and listening. Still, self-knowledge is not always perfect. We can misunderstand our motives or make mistakes about our attitudes. The main question is how we learn about ourselves and how trustworthy that learning is.
key_ideas: Self-knowledge is about knowing your own mental states, such as feelings, beliefs, desires, and intentions.
Some philosophers think self-knowledge is especially safe or reliable, while others point out that people can misunderstand themselves.
There are different ways to learn about your mind: looking inward, thinking about the world, interpreting your behavior, or expressing what you feel.
Some philosophers think self-knowledge is special because you are the person making choices and commitments.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding your own mind can help you think clearly, make plans, explain your actions, and notice when you may need help. It also helps us understand why people sometimes trust someone’s report about their own feelings while still recognizing that self-understanding can be difficult.

important_terms.definition: Knowledge about your own thoughts, feelings, beliefs, wants, and intentions.
The idea that a person may have a special way of knowing their own mind.
Paying attention to your own thoughts or feelings to learn what is happening inside you.
The power to choose, think, and act rather than merely having things happen to you.
A special expectation that people should usually be trusted when they describe their own thoughts or feelings.

questions_to_think_about: Can you ever be mistaken about what you feel or believe?
Is paying attention to your feelings the only way to learn about them?
Why might other people usually listen when you explain your own feelings?
Could thinking about a question change what you believed before?

summaries.example: Suppose you are asked whether you believe a difficult exam will go well. One approach says you should inspect an inner feeling or thought. Another says you should consider the exam itself—its difficulty, your preparation, and the evidence—and then judge whether you believe it will go well. A third view says that making a rational judgment about the exam is already closely connected to having, and knowing that you have, the corresponding belief. These approaches may explain different aspects of self-knowledge, and each faces objections: reflection can be mistaken, and considering the evidence may create a new belief rather than reveal an earlier one.
summaries.summary: The philosophical study of self-knowledge concerns knowledge of one’s own mental states, not primarily knowledge of a persisting personal self. The central issue is whether such knowledge is distinctive, and, if so, in what respect. One possibility is epistemic security: self-knowledge may be more secure than perceptual knowledge, although broad claims of infallibility or omniscience are difficult to defend. A second possibility is method. Traditional theories appeal to introspection, understood as inward attention, while transparency theories hold that one can determine what one believes by considering the states of affairs that the belief represents. Other theories treat self-knowledge as interpretation of thoughts, feelings, behavior, and context. Rationalist accounts connect it to the requirements of rational thinking; agentialist accounts connect it to responsibility and authorship of beliefs and intentions; expressivist accounts focus on avowals that directly express mental states and may carry first-person authority. These approaches differ over whether self-knowledge is inferential, non-inferential, empirically grounded, normatively guaranteed, or partly constituted by the subject’s rational activity. Doubts arise from ordinary mistakes, the relational character of beliefs and desires, and psychological findings about reports of unconscious influences. The entry presents these disputes without treating any one account as settled.
key_ideas: The distinctiveness of self-knowledge can concern its security, its method, the subject’s agency, or the authority given to first-person reports; these are different claims.
Strong claims such as infallibility and omniscience are generally rejected for all mental states, since people can be wrong about their own beliefs, desires, and motives.
Introspection is only one proposed method. Transparency accounts say that one may determine what one believes by considering the world or evidence represented by the belief.
Some theories treat self-knowledge as inferential or interpretive, while rationalist and agentialist theories connect it to rationality, responsibility, and commitment.
Expressivist theories emphasize avowals such as “I am in pain,” which may express a mental state directly rather than report it on the basis of separate evidence.
Psychological research and philosophical arguments raise doubts about how reliable introspection is, but they do not settle the scope of its reliability.
summaries.why_it_matters: Theories of self-knowledge affect major questions in epistemology, philosophy of mind, and moral psychology. They bear on whether people can know their own reasons, beliefs, and intentions; whether self-understanding is a form of observation or agency; and why first-person reports receive special treatment. The issue also matters practically: recognizing both the authority and fallibility of self-reports can improve reflection without assuming that every introspective judgment is automatically correct.

important_terms.definition: Knowledge of one’s own mental states, including sensations, emotions, beliefs, desires, and intentions.
The claim that self-knowledge has a special epistemic position compared with knowledge of the external world or other minds.
Attention directed toward one’s own mental states, traditionally understood as a kind of inner observation.
The epistemic status of a belief: how secure, justified, or reliable it is as knowledge.
A proposed first-personal route to self-knowledge, including inward attention or considering what a mental state represents.
The capacity to form and revise beliefs and intentions in response to reasons, rather than merely undergoing mental states.
The ordinary social-linguistic presumption that a person’s sincere statements about their own mental states should generally be accepted.
The position that knowing one’s beliefs or desires often requires interpreting thoughts, feelings, behavior, and circumstances.

questions_to_think_about: Does the possibility of error show that self-knowledge is not special, or can it still be more secure than other knowledge?
When you answer a question about what you believe, are you discovering an existing belief or forming a new judgment?
Can a person be responsible for regulating a belief or intention without having some knowledge of it?
Should a sincere first-person report be treated as authoritative even when other evidence conflicts with it?
Which account best explains knowledge of sensations, and which best explains knowledge of beliefs or intentions?

summaries.example: You tell a friend, “I really want to join the soccer team.” How could you know that? You might notice excitement when you imagine practice, look at your recent choices, or think about why joining matters to you. One philosopher might call this self-interpretation: using clues to understand your desire. Another might say that deciding to join already shows something about your intention. A different view says you should consider the team and its activities, almost as if you are looking outward rather than inspecting your mind. Each method may work in some cases, but none is obviously perfect.
summaries.summary: Self-knowledge is knowledge of your own mental states: what you think, feel, believe, want, and intend. Philosophers have long asked whether this knowledge differs from knowledge of objects or other people’s minds. Several answers are possible. Self-knowledge might be more secure, though people are not always infallible or aware of every mental state. It might involve a first-personal method, such as introspection, in which you attend to your own experience. But transparency theories suggest that, to discover what you believe, you may instead consider the subject your belief is about. Other philosophers describe self-knowledge as self-interpretation, using inner speech, feelings, behavior, and context as clues. Rationalist theories connect it to the demands of rational thought, while agentialist theories emphasize that beliefs and intentions are connected to responsibility and choice. Expressivist theories focus on statements that directly express a person’s mental state and explain why others often accept such statements. There are also serious doubts about the special status of self-knowledge. People sometimes misread their motives, and research suggests that they can be poor at identifying unconscious causes of their decisions. The entry compares these competing ideas rather than presenting one final answer.
key_ideas: Philosophers disagree about whether self-knowledge is special because it is more reliable, uses a unique method, involves agency, or receives special social respect.
Being aware of a mental state does not guarantee perfect knowledge of it. People can be wrong about what they believe, want, or feel.
Introspection is one proposed method, but transparency theories say that learning what you believe may involve considering the world and the evidence for a claim.
Some theories explain self-knowledge through interpretation and inference, while others connect it to rational thinking or responsibility for one’s attitudes.
A person’s statement such as “I am in pain” may be treated as authoritative because it directly expresses a state or because social rules tell us to defer to the speaker.
Studies of people’s explanations for their choices create doubts about introspection, especially concerning influences that are not conscious.
summaries.why_it_matters: Self-knowledge matters because it influences how we understand responsibility, decision-making, communication, and personal growth. It can explain why your own report about a feeling is often given special weight, while also showing why reflection should remain open to mistakes. Studying the topic teaches an important philosophical lesson: a question that seems familiar—“What do I think or want?”—can have several difficult answers.

important_terms.definition: Knowing your own thoughts, feelings, beliefs, desires, or intentions.
The proposed special advantage people may have in learning about their own mental states.
Trying to learn about your mind by directing attention toward your own thoughts and feelings.
How well a belief is protected from error or supported as knowledge.
A way of finding out about your own mind that is available to you as the person having the mental state.
The ability to guide beliefs and intentions through reasons and choices.
The usual practice of treating people as especially reliable about their own mental states.
Figuring out what you believe or want by making sense of your thoughts, feelings, behavior, and situation.

questions_to_think_about: Why might someone honestly give an incorrect description of their own belief or motive?
Is a first-person report authoritative because the speaker knows more, or because conversation normally works that way?
Can looking at evidence about the world tell you what you already believed?
Are beliefs and intentions things we observe, or things we partly create through rational activity?
Would a theory that explains knowledge of pain also explain knowledge of a long-held desire?
